title: Why Algorithms Matter
explanation: An algorithm is a step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. Some recipes are faster than others. A good algorithm can do in seconds what a bad one takes hours to do.
analogy: Two cooks making the same dish: one works smart, one works hard. The smart cook finishes first with less effort. Good algorithms are the smart approach.
example: Finding a name in a phone book: reading every page vs opening to the middle and narrowing down. Same result, vastly different time.
why_it_matters: When computers handle millions of items, algorithm choice can mean the difference between instant results and waiting for days.
checkpoint_question: Can two different algorithms solve the exact same problem?
expected_answer: Yes! Many algorithms can solve the same problem. They differ in speed, memory use, and simplicity. Choosing the right one depends on your needs.
common_mistake: Thinking the first solution that works is good enough. Often a better algorithm exists.
key_insight: The best programmers know many algorithms and can pick the right tool for each job.

title: Linear Search: Check One by One
explanation: Linear search checks each item from start to end until it finds what you're looking for. Simple but can be slow for large lists.
analogy: Like finding your keys by checking every pocket, every drawer, every surface - one at a time until you find them.
example: Finding 7 in [3, 1, 7, 9]: check 3 (no), check 1 (no), check 7 (yes!). Found after 3 checks.
why_it_matters: It's the simplest search and works on any list, even unsorted ones. It's your starting point for understanding search.
checkpoint_question: In the worst case, how many items do you check with linear search?
expected_answer: All of them. If the item is last or not there at all, you check every single item.
common_mistake: Using linear search on large sorted data. If it's sorted, binary search is much faster.
key_insight: Linear search is perfect for small lists or unsorted data. Don't optimize until you need to.

title: Binary Search: Divide and Conquer
explanation: Binary search works on sorted lists. Check the middle: if target is smaller, search left half; if larger, search right half. Repeat. Each step eliminates half the items!
analogy: Like the 'high or low' number guessing game. Each guess eliminates half the possibilities.
example: Finding 7 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]: Middle is 5. 7 > 5, search right half [7, 9]. Middle is 7. Found!
why_it_matters: Binary search is incredibly fast. Finding an item in 1 billion entries takes only about 30 checks!
checkpoint_question: Why must the list be sorted for binary search to work?
expected_answer: Because we use the middle element to decide which half to search. If the list isn't sorted, we can't know which half contains our target.
common_mistake: Using binary search on unsorted data. It will give wrong results without warning!
key_insight: Log base 2 of 1 billion is about 30. That's how many comparisons binary search needs for a billion items!

title: Why Sorting Matters
explanation: Sorting puts items in order: smallest to largest, A to Z, newest to oldest. Many tasks become easier once data is sorted - like binary search, finding duplicates, or displaying data neatly.
analogy: A messy room vs an organized one. Finding anything in an organized room is faster.
example: Unsorted: [5, 2, 8, 1]. Sorted: [1, 2, 5, 8]. Now you can use binary search, find min/max instantly, display nicely.
why_it_matters: Sorting is one of the most fundamental operations. Many algorithms require sorted data to work efficiently.
checkpoint_question: Name two things that become easier when data is sorted.
expected_answer: Binary search (only works on sorted data), finding minimum/maximum (just look at ends), finding duplicates (duplicates are next to each other), displaying data nicely.
common_mistake: Sorting when you don't need to. Sorting takes time. Only sort if it helps your goal.
code:
numbers = [5, 2, 8, 1]

# Built-in sort (modifies original)
numbers.sort()
print(numbers)  # [1, 2, 5, 8]

# Sorted function (returns new list)
original = [5, 2, 8, 1]
ordered = sorted(original)
print(ordered)   # [1, 2, 5, 8]
print(original)  # [5, 2, 8, 1] unchanged
key_insight: Python's built-in sort is highly optimized. Use it unless you're learning how sorting works.

title: Bubble Sort: Simple but Slow
explanation: Bubble sort repeatedly walks through the list, compares neighbors, and swaps if they're in wrong order. Larger items 'bubble up' to the end. Simple to understand but slow for large lists.
analogy: Like sorting a row of people by height by only swapping neighbors. The tallest person eventually ends up at the end.
example: [5, 2, 8, 1]: Compare 5&2 (swap→[2,5,8,1]), 5&8 (ok), 8&1 (swap→[2,5,1,8]). 8 is now at end. Repeat for remaining.
why_it_matters: It's easy to understand, making it a great learning tool. But it's too slow for real use on large data.
checkpoint_question: Why is bubble sort called 'bubble' sort?
expected_answer: Large values 'bubble up' to the top (end of the list) like bubbles rising in water. Each pass pushes the largest unsorted item to its final position.
common_mistake: Using bubble sort for large data. It's O(n²) - 10x more items means 100x more work!
key_insight: Bubble sort is rarely used in practice. It's mainly educational. Real programs use faster algorithms.

title: How Fast is Fast? Big O Basics
explanation: Big O describes how algorithm time grows as input grows. O(n) means time grows proportionally with input size. O(n²) means doubling input quadruples time. It helps compare algorithms without running them.
analogy: Like car fuel efficiency. One car uses fuel proportionally to distance (O(n)). Another uses fuel proportional to distance squared (O(n²)). For long trips, the difference is huge.
example: Linear search is O(n): 1000 items ≈ 1000 checks. Bubble sort is O(n²): 1000 items ≈ 1,000,000 comparisons!
why_it_matters: Big O tells you if an algorithm will scale. An O(n²) algorithm that works for 100 items might be unusable for 1,000,000.
checkpoint_question: If an O(n²) algorithm takes 1 second for 1000 items, how long for 2000 items?
expected_answer: About 4 seconds. Doubling n means n² quadruples (2² = 4). That's why O(n²) algorithms scale poorly.
common_mistake: Ignoring Big O for small data. For tiny inputs, any algorithm is fast enough. Big O matters when data grows.
key_insight: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n). Know this order!

title: Understanding O(1), O(n), O(n²)
explanation: O(1): instant, same time always. O(n): time equals input size. O(n²): time is input squared. For 1000 items: O(1)=1 operation, O(n)=1000, O(n²)=1,000,000!
analogy: O(1): checking if a light is on. O(n): counting people in a line. O(n²): shaking hands with everyone at a party (everyone meets everyone).
example: Array access is O(1): items[500] is instant. Finding max is O(n): must check all. Bubble sort is O(n²): compares all pairs.
why_it_matters: Understanding these basics lets you predict how code behaves at scale.
checkpoint_question: Why is dictionary lookup O(1) but list searching O(n)?
expected_answer: Dictionaries use hashing to jump directly to the item. Lists must check items one by one from the start. Different structures, different speeds.
common_mistake: Thinking O(n²) is fine. For 10 items, yes. For 10,000 items, it's 100 million operations!
key_insight: When you see nested loops, think O(n²). When you see halving (like binary search), think O(log n).

title: What is Recursion?
explanation: Recursion is when a function calls itself. It solves a problem by breaking it into smaller versions of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a 'base case' to stop.
analogy: Like Russian nesting dolls. To unpack all dolls, you keep opening smaller ones until you reach the smallest (base case).
example: Factorial: 5! = 5 × 4!. What's 4!? It's 4 × 3!. Eventually reaches 1! = 1 (base case), then multiplies back up.
why_it_matters: Many problems are naturally recursive: file systems, tree structures, mathematical sequences.
checkpoint_question: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
expected_answer: It calls itself forever until the program crashes (stack overflow). The base case is what stops the recursion.
common_mistake: Forgetting the base case. Always define when recursion should stop!
code:
# Factorial: n! = n × (n-1)!
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:        # Base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)  # Recursive call

print(factorial(5))  # 120

# How it works:
# factorial(5) = 5 × factorial(4)
#              = 5 × 4 × factorial(3)
#              = 5 × 4 × 3 × factorial(2)
#              = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × factorial(1)
#              = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120
space_complexity: O(n) - each call uses stack space
key_insight: Every recursive solution has a loop solution. Choose based on clarity. Trees and graphs often feel more natural with recursion.

title: Breaking Down Problems
explanation: Complex problems become simple when broken into smaller pieces. Solve each small piece, then combine the solutions. This is the heart of algorithmic thinking.
analogy: Eating an elephant: one bite at a time. Building a house: foundation, walls, roof - not all at once.
example: Sort a million numbers: split into halves, sort each half, merge results. Sorting 500,000 is easier than 1,000,000.
why_it_matters: This 'divide and conquer' approach solves seemingly impossible problems by making them manageable.
checkpoint_question: Why is dividing a problem into smaller parts helpful?
expected_answer: Smaller problems are easier to solve and understand. You can reuse solutions. You can tackle pieces in parallel. Complexity becomes manageable.
common_mistake: Trying to solve everything at once. Step back and identify smaller subproblems first.
code:
# Problem: sum all numbers in a list

# Iterative approach
def sum_list(items):
    total = 0
    for item in items:
        total += item
    return total

# Divide and conquer approach
def sum_recursive(items):
    if len(items) == 0:
        return 0
    if len(items) == 1:
        return items[0]
    mid = len(items) // 2
    left_sum = sum_recursive(items[:mid])
    right_sum = sum_recursive(items[mid:])
    return left_sum + right_sum
key_insight: Merge sort, quicksort, and binary search all use divide and conquer. It's one of the most powerful algorithm design strategies.

title: Finding Paths in Graphs
explanation: Graphs represent connections (like maps or social networks). Common questions: Is there a path between two points? What's the shortest path? Algorithms like BFS (breadth-first search) and DFS (depth-first search) answer these.
analogy: BFS: exploring a city level by level - first all neighbors, then their neighbors. DFS: going down one street as far as possible before backtracking.
example: BFS finds shortest path in an unweighted maze. DFS checks if a path exists. GPS uses weighted shortest-path algorithms.
why_it_matters: Graph algorithms power navigation apps, social networks (friend suggestions), and many optimization problems.
checkpoint_question: Why does BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
expected_answer: BFS explores level by level - all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, etc. The first time it reaches the target, that's the shortest path because closer nodes are explored first.
common_mistake: Using DFS to find shortest path. DFS might find a path, but not necessarily the shortest one.
key_insight: BFS uses a queue (first in, first out). DFS uses a stack (last in, first out) or recursion.

title: Remembering Past Work
explanation: Dynamic programming solves problems by breaking them into smaller subproblems, solving each once, and storing results. When the same subproblem appears again, you just look up the answer instead of recalculating.
analogy: Like using a cheat sheet for math. Calculate 7×8 once, write it down. Next time you need it, just look it up.
example: Fibonacci: fib(5) needs fib(4) and fib(3). fib(4) needs fib(3). Without storing, you calculate fib(3) twice. With DP, calculate once, reuse.
why_it_matters: DP transforms exponentially slow solutions into fast polynomial ones. Many optimization problems use DP.
checkpoint_question: What's the main idea behind dynamic programming?
expected_answer: Solve each subproblem only once and store (memoize) the result. When you need that answer again, look it up instead of recalculating.
common_mistake: Not recognizing overlapping subproblems. If subproblems are calculated multiple times, DP helps.
time_complexity: Often O(n²) or O(n) instead of O(2^n)
key_insight: Two approaches: top-down (memoization - add caching to recursion) or bottom-up (build table from smallest subproblems).

title: Picking the Right Algorithm
explanation: Different problems need different algorithms. Searching? Consider binary search if sorted. Shortest path? BFS for unweighted, Dijkstra for weighted. There's no universal 'best' - it depends on your problem and constraints.
analogy: Choosing the right vehicle: bike for short trips, car for medium, plane for long. Each is best for its situation.
example: Need to sort? Use built-in sort (optimized). Need shortest path? Use BFS. Need to find duplicates? Use a set or dictionary.
why_it_matters: Knowing multiple algorithms lets you pick the right tool. The best programmers have a toolbox of algorithms.
checkpoint_question: When would you use linear search over binary search?
expected_answer: When the data is unsorted. Binary search requires sorted data. For small datasets or one-time searches on unsorted data, linear search is simpler and fine.
common_mistake: Over-engineering simple problems. Sometimes a basic loop is all you need.
key_insight: Learn common algorithms well. Most problems are variations of classics: search, sort, graph traversal, dynamic programming.

title: Merge Sort: Divide and Conquer
explanation: Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges the sorted halves. It's consistently O(n log n) - no worst case slowdowns like quicksort. The trade-off is it needs extra memory.
analogy: Like sorting two decks of cards: sort each deck separately, then merge them by comparing the top cards and taking the smaller one.
why_it_matters: Merge sort is stable (preserves order of equal items) and consistent. It's the go-to when stability matters or data is too large for memory (external sorting).
checkpoint_question: Why does merge sort always take O(n log n) time?
expected_answer: It always splits in half (log n levels) and merges all n items at each level. No matter the input order, it does the same work. Quicksort's O(n²) worst case comes from bad pivot choices - merge sort avoids this.
common_mistake: Forgetting merge sort needs O(n) extra space for merging. If memory is tight, in-place sorts might be better.
key_insight: Python's built-in sort (Timsort) is a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort - it gets the best of both worlds.

title: Quicksort: Fast in Practice
explanation: Quicksort picks a 'pivot' element, partitions the array into elements smaller and larger than pivot, then sorts each partition. Average O(n log n), worst O(n²) with bad pivots. Despite this, it's often fastest in practice due to cache efficiency.
analogy: Like organizing books: pick one (pivot), put shorter books left, taller books right. Repeat for each pile until sorted.
example: Pivot = 5 in [3,7,5,2,8]: Partition → [3,2] [5] [7,8]. Recursively sort [3,2] → [2,3] and [7,8] stays. Result: [2,3,5,7,8].
why_it_matters: Quicksort is used in many language standard libraries because it's fast in practice, despite theoretical worst case.
checkpoint_question: What causes quicksort's O(n²) worst case?
expected_answer: When pivot is always the smallest or largest element - like picking the first element in an already-sorted array. Each partition removes only one element, giving n levels instead of log n.
common_mistake: Always picking the first or last element as pivot. Use random pivot or median-of-three to avoid worst case.
time_complexity: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst
key_insight: Quicksort is in-place (doesn't need extra array) and cache-friendly. For most data, it beats merge sort despite worse worst-case.

title: Hash-Based Lookup: O(1) Search
explanation: Hash tables (dictionaries) provide near-instant lookup by converting keys to array positions using a hash function. Instead of searching through items, you compute where an item should be and go directly there.
analogy: Like a coat check: your name is converted to a ticket number (hash). To get your coat, give the number and they go directly to that spot.
example: Looking up 'alice' in a million-user database: hash('alice') = 42847. Go directly to slot 42847. No scanning needed.
why_it_matters: Hash tables are why dictionaries, sets, and database indexes are fast. Understanding them helps you choose the right data structure.
checkpoint_question: What happens when two keys hash to the same position (collision)?
expected_answer: The hash table handles it, usually by storing both items at that position (in a list or by probing nearby slots). More collisions = slower lookup, which is why good hash functions spread keys evenly.
common_mistake: Assuming O(1) is guaranteed. With many collisions, it degrades toward O(n). Use good hash functions and sizing.
code:
# Python dict uses hash table internally
users = {}
users['alice'] = {'email': 'alice@mail.com'}  # O(1)
users['bob'] = {'email': 'bob@mail.com'}      # O(1)

# Instant lookup
print(users['alice'])  # O(1) - no matter how big

# How hashing works conceptually:
# hash('alice') → 42847
# store at position 42847 % table_size

# Check membership
if 'alice' in users:  # O(1) - uses hash lookup
    print('Found!')
key_insight: Sets are hash tables too - they just store keys without values. 'x in my_set' is O(1), 'x in my_list' is O(n).

title: Depth-First Search: Explore Deep First
explanation: DFS explores as far as possible down each path before backtracking. It uses a stack (or recursion). Good for: finding any path, detecting cycles, topological sorting. Not for: finding shortest path.
analogy: Like exploring a maze by always turning right. Go as far as you can, then backtrack and try another path. You'll eventually cover everything.
example: In a file system, DFS would fully explore one folder (and all its subfolders) before moving to the next folder.
why_it_matters: DFS is foundational for many graph algorithms: cycle detection, finding connected components, topological sort.
checkpoint_question: When would you choose DFS over BFS?
expected_answer: When you don't need the shortest path, just any path. Also when exploring deeply - like checking if a path exists, finding cycles, or traversing trees/file systems. DFS uses less memory for deep graphs.
common_mistake: Using DFS when you need shortest path. DFS finds a path, but possibly a long one. Use BFS for shortest in unweighted graphs.
time_complexity: O(V + E) - visits all vertices and edges
space_complexity: O(V) for visited set and recursion stack
key_insight: DFS naturally uses recursion. If recursion is limited, use an explicit stack instead.

title: Greedy Algorithms: Best Choice Now
explanation: Greedy algorithms make the locally best choice at each step, hoping to find a global optimum. They're simple and fast but don't always give the best answer. Works for some problems (coin change with standard coins), fails for others.
analogy: Like climbing a mountain by always going uphill. Works if there's one peak, but you might get stuck on a small hill missing the tallest peak.
example: Making change for 67¢ with US coins: take as many quarters (2), then dimes (1), nickels (1), pennies (2). Greedy works here because coin values are designed for it.
why_it_matters: Greedy is fast when it works. Recognizing when it works (and when it doesn't) is key to efficient algorithm design.
checkpoint_question: Why doesn't greedy always work?
expected_answer: A locally best choice might prevent finding the globally best solution. Making change with coins [1, 3, 4] for 6: greedy gives 4+1+1 (3 coins), but optimal is 3+3 (2 coins). The best immediate choice wasn't best overall.
common_mistake: Assuming greedy is correct without proof. Always verify greedy works for your specific problem or use DP instead.
code:
# Greedy coin change (works for US coins)
def make_change(amount, coins=[25, 10, 5, 1]):
    result = []
    for coin in coins:
        while amount >= coin:
            result.append(coin)
            amount -= coin
    return result

print(make_change(67))  # [25, 25, 10, 5, 1, 1]

# Doesn't work for all coin systems!
# coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6
# Greedy: [4, 1, 1] = 3 coins
# Optimal: [3, 3] = 2 coins
time_complexity: Usually O(n) or O(n log n)
key_insight: Greedy works when a problem has 'greedy choice property' (local optimum leads to global) and 'optimal substructure' (optimal solution contains optimal sub-solutions).

title: Space Complexity: Memory Matters Too
explanation: Space complexity measures memory usage. Some algorithms are fast but use lots of memory (merge sort). Others are slower but use little memory (bubble sort). Both time AND space matter, especially with limited resources.
analogy: A chef can cook faster with more counter space (memory), but a small kitchen requires working more efficiently with less space.
example: Merge sort: O(n) extra space for temporary arrays. Quicksort: O(log n) stack space. For 1 billion items, that's 1 billion vs ~30 extra slots.
why_it_matters: Memory is finite. An algorithm that's fast but uses too much RAM might crash or slow down due to swapping.
checkpoint_question: Why might you choose a slower algorithm that uses less space?
expected_answer: If memory is limited, a slower in-place algorithm might be necessary. On embedded devices, mobile apps, or with massive datasets, memory efficiency matters more than raw speed.
common_mistake: Ignoring space complexity. An O(n) time algorithm using O(n²) space can be worse than O(n²) time using O(1) space for large n.
key_insight: In-place algorithms modify the input instead of creating copies. They save memory but change the original data - sometimes undesirable.

title: NP-Hard Problems: When Algorithms Struggle
explanation: Some problems are so hard that no fast algorithm is known (and probably doesn't exist). The Traveling Salesman Problem, optimal scheduling, and many others are 'NP-hard'. For these, we use approximations or heuristics instead of exact solutions.
analogy: Like trying to try every possible route for a delivery truck. With 20 stops, there are over 2 quadrillion possibilities. No shortcut exists.
example: Traveling Salesman: visit all cities with shortest total distance. For 50 cities, checking all routes would take longer than the universe's age.
why_it_matters: Recognizing NP-hard problems saves time. Don't search for a fast exact solution - use approximations instead.
checkpoint_question: If a problem is NP-hard, what should you do?
expected_answer: Accept you won't find the perfect solution quickly. Use approximation algorithms (get close to optimal), heuristics (rules of thumb), or solve smaller versions. Good enough is often good enough.
common_mistake: Trying to brute force NP-hard problems. Scale kills you. Even supercomputers can't help with problems that grow exponentially.
code:
# Traveling Salesman - brute force (infeasible for large n)
import itertools

def tsp_brute(distances):
    cities = list(range(len(distances)))
    shortest = float('inf')
    
    for route in itertools.permutations(cities):
        total = sum(distances[route[i]][route[i+1]] 
                   for i in range(len(route)-1))
        shortest = min(shortest, total)
    
    return shortest

# For 10 cities: 3.6 million routes - slow
# For 20 cities: 2.4 quintillion routes - impossible

# Real solution: use approximation algorithms
# like nearest neighbor, genetic algorithms, etc.
key_insight: P vs NP is an unsolved problem worth $1 million. If P=NP, many 'hard' problems would have fast solutions. Most experts believe P≠NP.

title: Algorithmic Problem Solving
explanation: Solving algorithm problems: 1) Understand the problem fully. 2) Think of simple examples. 3) Identify patterns. 4) Start with brute force. 5) Look for optimizations. 6) Code it. 7) Test edge cases.
analogy: Like solving a puzzle: first understand what you're building, try simple pieces, find patterns, start rough, refine until done.
example: Problem: find pairs that sum to target. Think: brute force = check all pairs O(n²). Optimize: use a set to check if complement exists O(n).
why_it_matters: This systematic approach works for any algorithm problem. It's how professionals solve new challenges.
checkpoint_question: Why start with brute force even if it's slow?
expected_answer: Brute force proves you understand the problem and gives a correct (if slow) baseline. It often reveals patterns that lead to optimization. It's easier to improve correct-but-slow than to fix fast-but-wrong.
common_mistake: Jumping to clever solutions before understanding the problem. Slow and correct beats fast and wrong.
key_insight: Practice patterns: two pointers, sliding window, hash for lookup, sort then search, dynamic programming. Most problems use one of these.

title: Two Pointers: Efficient Array Scanning
explanation: Two pointers use two indices moving through an array - often from both ends toward the middle, or both from the start at different speeds. This reduces many O(n²) problems to O(n).
analogy: Like two people searching a bookshelf from opposite ends, meeting in the middle. Faster than one person checking every book.
example: Is array a palindrome? Check if first equals last, then second equals second-to-last, etc. Two pointers moving inward.
why_it_matters: Two pointers turn quadratic problems into linear ones. It's a fundamental technique for array and string problems.
checkpoint_question: When is two pointers useful?
expected_answer: When you need to find pairs or compare elements at different positions. Works especially well on sorted arrays or when looking for conditions at both ends.
common_mistake: Using two pointers on unsorted data when order matters. Often you need to sort first.
key_insight: Two pointers work because moving a pointer eliminates many possibilities at once. On sorted data, you know the direction to move.

title: Sliding Window: Subarray Problems
explanation: Sliding window maintains a 'window' over part of an array, sliding it along. Instead of recalculating everything for each position, you add the new element and remove the old. Turns O(n×k) into O(n).
analogy: Like viewing through a frame that slides across a picture. You don't look at the whole picture each time - just what enters and exits the frame.
example: Max sum of any 3 consecutive elements. Instead of summing 3 elements at each position, slide: subtract the element leaving, add the element entering.
why_it_matters: Any problem about consecutive elements or substrings often benefits from sliding window. Very common pattern.
checkpoint_question: Why is sliding window faster than recalculating each time?
expected_answer: Most of the window stays the same. You only process the change: one element enters, one leaves. This is O(1) per move instead of O(k) to recalculate k elements.
common_mistake: Forgetting to handle the initial window setup. Often need special handling for the first k elements.
code:
def max_sum_subarray(nums, k):
    """Find max sum of k consecutive elements"""
    # Initial window sum
    window_sum = sum(nums[:k])
    max_sum = window_sum
    
    # Slide the window
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window_sum += nums[i]      # Add new element
        window_sum -= nums[i - k]  # Remove old element
        max_sum = max(max_sum, window_sum)
    
    return max_sum

# O(n) instead of O(n×k)
key_insight: Variable-width sliding windows expand/contract based on conditions. Fixed-width windows are simpler but less flexible.

title: Backtracking: Try and Undo
explanation: Backtracking explores possibilities by making choices, and if a choice leads to a dead end, it undoes (backtracks) and tries a different choice. Used for puzzles, permutations, and constraint problems.
analogy: Like solving a maze by trying paths. Hit a dead end? Go back to the last intersection and try another way.
example: Sudoku: try a number, continue solving. If you get stuck, backtrack and try a different number. Eventually find a valid solution or prove none exists.
why_it_matters: Many problems require exploring possibilities: generating combinations, solving puzzles, finding paths with constraints.
checkpoint_question: How is backtracking different from brute force?
expected_answer: Backtracking prunes - it abandons paths early when they can't lead to solutions. Brute force checks everything. Backtracking can be much faster by eliminating dead ends.
common_mistake: Not actually undoing the choice. After exploring a path, you must restore the state before trying another path.
code:
def generate_permutations(nums):
    """Generate all permutations via backtracking"""
    result = []
    
    def backtrack(current, remaining):
        if not remaining:  # Base case
            result.append(current[:])
            return
        
        for i, num in enumerate(remaining):
            # Make choice
            current.append(num)
            # Explore
            backtrack(current, remaining[:i] + remaining[i+1:])
            # Undo choice (backtrack)
            current.pop()
    
    backtrack([], nums)
    return result

# [1,2,3] → [[1,2,3], [1,3,2], [2,1,3], ...]
key_insight: The key to good backtracking is pruning early. The sooner you detect a dead end, the more work you skip.

title: Memoization: Remembering Results
explanation: Memoization stores results of expensive function calls. If called again with the same inputs, return the stored result instead of recalculating. Dramatically speeds up recursive algorithms with overlapping subproblems.
analogy: Like keeping a cheat sheet of problems you've already solved. When you see the same problem again, just look up the answer.
example: Fibonacci: fib(5) calls fib(3) multiple times. Without memo, you recalculate each time. With memo, calculate once and reuse.
why_it_matters: Memoization turns exponential algorithms into polynomial ones. It's the 'easy' version of dynamic programming.
checkpoint_question: What's the relationship between memoization and dynamic programming?
expected_answer: Memoization is top-down DP: start from the big problem, recurse down, cache results. Bottom-up DP builds from smallest problems up. Same idea, different direction.
common_mistake: Memoizing functions with side effects or that depend on external state. Only memoize pure functions where output depends only on inputs.
key_insight: @lru_cache in Python is a built-in memoization decorator. Just add it to a function and caching happens automatically.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm: Shortest Paths
explanation: Dijkstra finds the shortest path from one node to all others in a weighted graph. It greedily picks the closest unvisited node, updates distances to its neighbors, and repeats. Like BFS but for weighted edges.
analogy: Like planning the fastest route on a map. Always explore the road that gets you somewhere fastest, update your knowledge, repeat.
example: GPS navigation: cities are nodes, roads are edges with travel times as weights. Dijkstra finds the fastest route from your location to any destination.
why_it_matters: Dijkstra is the basis of GPS navigation, network routing, and many shortest-path applications. Fundamental algorithm.
checkpoint_question: Why doesn't Dijkstra work with negative edge weights?
expected_answer: Dijkstra assumes once you've found the shortest path to a node, you're done. Negative weights could make a longer-looking path actually shorter. Use Bellman-Ford for negative weights.
common_mistake: Using BFS for weighted graphs. BFS finds fewest edges, not shortest total distance. Dijkstra handles weights.
time_complexity: O((V + E) log V) with heap
key_insight: A* algorithm extends Dijkstra with a heuristic to guide search toward the goal. It's faster when you know the destination.

title: Stable vs Unstable Sorting
explanation: A stable sort preserves the original order of equal elements. If two items have the same key, they stay in their original relative order. Unstable sorts might rearrange equal elements.
analogy: Sorting a deck by suit. Stable: cards of the same suit stay in their original order. Unstable: same-suit cards might get shuffled.
example: Sort students by grade. Alice and Bob both have A. Stable: their original order is preserved. Unstable: Bob might end up before Alice.
why_it_matters: Stability matters when you sort by multiple criteria. Sort by name, then by grade - stability keeps names sorted within each grade.
checkpoint_question: When does stability matter?
expected_answer: When equal items have a meaningful secondary order. If you sort records by department, you want people with the same department to stay in their original order (perhaps alphabetical).
common_mistake: Assuming all sorts are stable. Quick sort is not stable. Merge sort is. Python's sort is stable.
code:
# Python's sort is stable!
students = [
    ('Alice', 'B'),
    ('Bob', 'A'),
    ('Charlie', 'B'),
    ('Diana', 'A')
]

# Sort by grade (second element)
students.sort(key=lambda s: s[1])

# Result: [('Bob', 'A'), ('Diana', 'A'), ('Alice', 'B'), ('Charlie', 'B')]
# Within each grade, original order preserved!
# Bob before Diana (both A), Alice before Charlie (both B)
key_insight: To sort by multiple criteria, sort by secondary criteria first, then primary. Stability preserves the secondary sort within primary groups.

title: Best, Average, and Worst Case
explanation: Algorithm performance varies with input. Best case: the ideal input. Worst case: the hardest input. Average case: typical inputs. We usually focus on worst case for guarantees, but average case matters for real usage.
analogy: Like travel time. Best case: no traffic. Worst case: accident on highway. Average: typical rush hour. You plan for worst but expect average.
example: Quick sort: average O(n log n), but worst O(n²) if already sorted. Binary search: best O(1) if middle element matches, worst O(log n).
why_it_matters: Knowing when algorithms perform badly helps you avoid those cases or choose different algorithms.
checkpoint_question: Why does quick sort have O(n²) worst case but O(n log n) average?
expected_answer: Worst case: bad pivot choices create unbalanced partitions. If pivot is always smallest/largest, you get n partitions of size n-1, n-2, etc. Average case: pivots are roughly middle, creating balanced splits.
common_mistake: Only considering best or average case. Worst case can be triggered by attackers or unlucky data.
code:
# Linear search
def find(arr, target):
    for i, item in enumerate(arr):
        if item == target:
            return i
    return -1

# Best case: O(1) - first element
find([5, 1, 2, 3], 5)  # Found immediately

# Worst case: O(n) - last or not found
find([1, 2, 3, 5], 5)  # Check all

# Average case: O(n/2) = O(n) - middle
# On average, check half the elements
key_insight: Quick sort's worst case can be avoided by random pivot selection. Random makes worst case exponentially unlikely.

title: Binary Search Variations
explanation: Binary search doesn't just find exact matches. Find first occurrence, last occurrence, insertion point, or closest value. The core idea (eliminate half each time) applies to many 'search in sorted space' problems.
analogy: The phone book trick works for more than finding a name. Find the first Smith, the last Smith, or where a new name should go.
example: Find first occurrence of 5 in [1,2,5,5,5,8]. Regular binary search might find any 5. Modified version continues searching left to find the first.
why_it_matters: Binary search patterns solve many problems: finding boundaries, searching in rotated arrays, minimizing/maximizing values.
checkpoint_question: How would you find where to insert a new element to keep the list sorted?
expected_answer: Binary search for the position where element would go. Python's bisect module does this. When search 'fails', the position where it stopped is the insertion point.
common_mistake: Off-by-one errors in boundary cases. Carefully handle when target equals mid element - do you want leftmost or rightmost?
code:
import bisect

sorted_list = [1, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8, 10]

# Find insertion point (leftmost)
bisect.bisect_left(sorted_list, 5)  # 2 (before first 5)

# Find insertion point (rightmost)
bisect.bisect_right(sorted_list, 5)  # 5 (after last 5)

# Insert while keeping sorted
bisect.insort(sorted_list, 6)  # Inserts 6 in right place
time_complexity: O(log n) - same as regular binary search
key_insight: Binary search on answer: if you can check 'is X achievable?' in O(n), you can find the minimum achievable X in O(n log range).

title: Topological Sort: Ordering Dependencies
explanation: Topological sort orders items so dependencies come before dependents. If task A must complete before B, A appears first. Used for build systems, course prerequisites, package dependencies.
analogy: Like getting dressed. Underwear before pants, pants before belt. Find an order where everything happens after its prerequisites.
example: Courses: Algebra before Calculus, Calculus before Physics. Topological sort gives a valid semester order.
why_it_matters: Any system with dependencies needs ordering. Build systems, task schedulers, spreadsheet calculations all use topological sort.
checkpoint_question: What if there's a cycle in the dependencies?
expected_answer: No valid ordering exists. If A requires B and B requires A, neither can come first. Topological sort detects cycles - if it can't order everything, there's a cycle.
common_mistake: Assuming there's always a valid order. Check for cycles first, or detect during the sort.
key_insight: Kahn's algorithm (shown) uses BFS. DFS-based approach: finish DFS for a node, add to front of result. Both work.

title: Prefix Sums: Fast Range Queries
explanation: Prefix sums precompute cumulative totals. To find sum of any range, subtract prefix sums: sum(i to j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]. O(1) per query after O(n) preprocessing.
analogy: Like odometer readings. To find distance between two points, subtract readings. Don't need to re-drive the route.
example: Array [1,2,3,4,5]. Prefix sums [1,3,6,10,15]. Sum of index 1-3? prefix[3] - prefix[0] = 10 - 1 = 9. Check: 2+3+4 = 9.
why_it_matters: Range sum is a common operation. With prefix sums, any range query is O(1). Essential for competitive programming and data processing.
checkpoint_question: What's the tradeoff of prefix sums?
expected_answer: O(n) preprocessing time and space for the prefix array. But then unlimited O(1) queries. Worth it if you query many times.
common_mistake: Rebuilding prefix array after every array update. For frequent updates, use different structures (segment tree, Fenwick tree).
code:
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]

# Build prefix sums
prefix = [0]  # Start with 0 for easy indexing
for num in nums:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + num)
# prefix = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25, 31]

# Sum from index i to j (inclusive)
def range_sum(i, j):
    return prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i]

range_sum(2, 5)  # 4+1+5+9 = 19
# prefix[6] - prefix[2] = 23 - 4 = 19 ✓
key_insight: 2D prefix sums work similarly for rectangle sums in matrices. Four prefix values give any rectangle sum.

title: Counting Sort: When Values Are Limited
explanation: If values are in a small range (0 to k), count occurrences of each value, then reconstruct the sorted array. O(n+k) time - faster than comparison sorts when k is small.
analogy: Sorting a deck of cards by making 13 piles (one per rank), then collecting piles in order. No comparisons needed.
example: Ages of 1000 people (0-120). Make 121 buckets. Put each age in its bucket. Read buckets in order. O(1000 + 121) vs O(1000 × 10) for comparison sort.
why_it_matters: When applicable, counting sort is linear time. Know when the problem structure allows faster-than-O(n log n) sorting.
checkpoint_question: Why can't counting sort be used for sorting strings?
expected_answer: The 'range' of possible strings is effectively infinite. You'd need a bucket for every possible string. Counting sort needs a small, bounded value range.
common_mistake: Using counting sort when range is huge. Sorting 10 numbers in range 0 to 1 million wastes space. Use comparison sort instead.
code:
def counting_sort(arr, max_val):
    # Count occurrences
    count = [0] * (max_val + 1)
    for num in arr:
        count[num] += 1
    
    # Reconstruct sorted array
    result = []
    for val in range(max_val + 1):
        result.extend([val] * count[val])
    
    return result

# Example: grades 0-100
grades = [85, 92, 78, 85, 90, 78]
sorted_grades = counting_sort(grades, 100)
# [78, 78, 85, 85, 90, 92]
time_complexity: O(n + k) where k is the range
key_insight: Radix sort uses counting sort on each digit, sorting numbers of any size in O(d × (n + b)) where d is digits and b is base.

title: Union-Find: Connected Components
explanation: Union-Find tracks which elements are in the same group. Union: merge two groups. Find: check if two elements are in the same group. Near-O(1) operations with path compression and union by rank.
analogy: Like tracking friend groups. When two people become friends, their entire friend groups merge. Quickly ask: are A and B in the same group?
example: Network connectivity: edges connect computers. After adding edges, quickly answer: can computer A reach computer B? (Are they in the same component?)
why_it_matters: Union-Find is essential for Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, detecting cycles, and dynamic connectivity problems.
checkpoint_question: Why is union-find faster than BFS for connectivity queries?
expected_answer: BFS is O(V+E) per query. Union-find is nearly O(1) per query after processing edges. For many queries, union-find wins dramatically.
common_mistake: Not using path compression and union by rank. Without these optimizations, trees can become tall and operations slow.
key_insight: Union-find with path compression has inverse Ackermann time complexity - effectively constant for any realistic input size.
